claims.text: Overall tribocorrosion degradation in passivating high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by cyclic mechanical removal of the passive film followed by electrochemical repassivation.
The rate of electrochemical repassivation controls recovery after sliding removes the passive film.
Lowering pH, reducing inhibitor concentration, or reducing ambient oxygen will impair repassivation kinetics.
Under constant wear conditions, impaired repassivation will make corrosion a more dominant component of tribocorrosion degradation.
Impaired repassivation will increase cumulative mass loss relative to an efficiently repassivating baseline.
An AlCrTiZrMo-based high-entropy alloy can be processed to form a stable protective surface oxide film.
The processed AlCrTiZrMo-based material has high mechanical strength under standard conditions.
The processed AlCrTiZrMo-based material has good corrosion resistance under standard conditions.
Holding normal load, sliding speed, temperature, and other variables constant while varying electrolyte conditions provides a controlled comparison of repassivation propensity.
Mechanical sliding removes the protective passive film.
Slower repassivation leaves exposed metal more susceptible to accelerated corrosion.
An imbalance between passive-film removal and regeneration increases overall degradation.
In the repassivation-impaired condition, the corrosion-induced degradation component will increase significantly relative to the wear-only component.
The prediction applies where wear and corrosion are simultaneously active.
The prediction may fail when wear is negligible.
The prediction may fail when intrinsic repassivation is too rapid to be changed by the selected electrolyte modification.
The quantitative shift between corrosion and wear contributions cannot be specified without repassivation-rate data.
Failure of the impaired-repassivation condition to produce a statistically significant increase in both the corrosion component and cumulative mass loss would falsify the proposed mechanism.
